I’ve always thought that people carry two kinds of time inside them: the time on the clocks, measured in hours and minutes, and the time inside the body, measured in rhythms—hunger, breath, fatigue, wonder. The first kind of time marches forward no matter what; the second kind arrives and retreats like tidewater. Some days feel long because the hours stretch and stretch, refusing to become memories. Other days collapse into minutes, as if something in the world folds them up and hides the seams.

I like to notice the small signals that tell me which kind of time is happening. A morning cup of coffee can turn into a long conversation with myself, slowly cooling while my thoughts rearrange themselves. The street outside my window can feel either sharp-edged and present—every leaf a bright fact—or blurred, like a dream projected onto glass. Music does it too: the same song can either keep pace with my heart or drag it behind, as if I’m following tracks through snow.

Maybe that’s what writing is for: to catch a particular moment of inner time before it slips away. You set down the sentence, and suddenly the day has a shape. Even if you can’t return to that exact feeling, you can revisit the contour of it—the way it leaned, the way it softened, the way it ended.
